questions.problem:
Suppose $n=-6-8m,$ where $m\in Z.$ Complete the following argument showing that $n$ is even.

The number $n$ is even since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =-6-8m \\  & =2({{field-1}}) \\  & ={{field-2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=$ {{field-3}}, which is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *even* if it can be written as $2a,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is even since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =-6-8m \\  & =2({{-3-4m}_{⏟}}_{a}) \\  & =2a,\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=-3-4m,$ which is an integer.

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=16k+6,$ where $k\in Z.$ Complete the following argument showing that $n$ is even.

The number $n$ is even since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =16k+6 \\  & =2({{field-1}}) \\  & ={{field-2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=$ {{field-3}}, which is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *even* if it can be written as $2a,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is even since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =16k+6 \\  & =2({{8k+3}_{⏟}}_{a}) \\  & =2a,\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=8k+3,$ which is an integer.

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=10m+4,$ where $m\in Z.$ Complete the following argument showing that $n$ is even.

The number $n$ is even since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =10m+4 \\  & =2({{field-1}}) \\  & ={{field-2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=$ {{field-3}}, which is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *even* if it can be written as $2a,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is even since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =10m+4 \\  & =2({{5m+2}_{⏟}}_{a}) \\  & =2a,\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=5m+2,$ which is an integer.

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=12-10v,$ where $v\in Z.$ Complete the following argument showing that $n$ is even.

The number $n$ is even since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =12-10v \\  & =2({{field-1}}) \\  & ={{field-2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=$ {{field-3}}, which is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *even* if it can be written as $2a,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is even since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =12-10v \\  & =2({{6-5v}_{⏟}}_{a}) \\  & =2a,\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=6-5v,$ which is an integer.

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=-10-30q,$ where $q\in Z.$ Complete the following argument showing that $n$ is even.

The number $n$ is even since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =-10-30q \\  & =2({{field-1}}) \\  & ={{field-2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=$ {{field-3}}, which is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *even* if it can be written as $2a,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is even since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =-10-30q \\  & =2({{-5-15q}_{⏟}}_{a}) \\  & =2a,\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=-5-15q,$ which is an integer.

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=5-6k,$ where $k\in Z.$ Complete the following argument showing that $n$ is odd.

The number $n$ is odd since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =5-6k \\  & =2({{field-1}})+1 \\  & ={{field-2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=$ {{field-3}}, which is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *odd* if it can be written as $2a+1,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is odd since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =5-6k \\  & =(-6k+4)+1 \\  & =2({{-3k+2}_{⏟}}_{a})+1 \\  & =2a+1,\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=-3k+2,$ which is an integer.

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=6q-3,$ where $q\in Z.$ Complete the following argument showing that $n$ is odd.

The number $n$ is odd since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =6q-3 \\  & =2({{field-1}})+1 \\  & ={{field-2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=$ {{field-3}}, which is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *odd* if it can be written as $2a+1,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is odd since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =6q-3 \\  & =(6q-4)+1 \\  & =2({{3q-2}_{⏟}}_{a})+1 \\  & =2a+1,\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=3q-2,$ which is an integer.

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=10p-1,$ where $p\in Z.$ Complete the following argument showing that $n$ is odd.

The number $n$ is odd since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =10p-1 \\  & =2({{field-1}})+1 \\  & ={{field-2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=$ {{field-3}}, which is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *odd* if it can be written as $2a+1,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is odd since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =10p-1 \\  & =(10p-2)+1 \\  & =2({{5p-1}_{⏟}}_{a})+1 \\  & =2a+1,\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=5p-1,$ which is an integer.

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=1-8p,$ where $p\in Z.$ Complete the following argument showing that $n$ is odd.

The number $n$ is odd since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =1-8p \\  & =2({{field-1}})+1 \\  & ={{field-2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=$ {{field-3}}, which is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *odd* if it can be written as $2a+1,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is odd since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =1-8p \\  & =(-8p)+1 \\  & =2({{-4p}_{⏟}}_{a})+1 \\  & =2a+1,\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=-4p,$ which is an integer.

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=3-10m,$ where $m\in Z.$ Complete the following argument showing that $n$ is odd.

The number $n$ is odd since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =3-10m \\  & =2({{field-1}})+1 \\  & ={{field-2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=$ {{field-3}}, which is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *odd* if it can be written as $2a+1,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is odd since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =3-10m \\  & =(-10m+2)+1 \\  & =2({{-5m+1}_{⏟}}_{a})+1 \\  & =2a+1,\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=6{m}^{5}+8{m}^{4}-1,$ where $m\in Z.$ Complete the following argument.

The number $n$ is {{field-1}} since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =6{m}^{5}+8{m}^{4}-1 \\  & =2({{field-2}})+1 \\  & ={{field-3}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=$ {{field-4}} is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *odd* if it can be written as $2a+1,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Now, note the following regarding the expression $6{m}^{5}+8{m}^{4}-1:$

- All terms, apart from the constant term, have a common factor of $2.$

- The constant term can be written as $-1=-2+1.$

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is $\text{odd}$ since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =6{m}^{5}+8{m}^{4}-1 \\  & =(6{m}^{5}+8{m}^{4}-2)+1 \\  & =2({{3{m}^{5}+4{m}^{4}-1}_{⏟}}_{a})+1 \\  & =2a+1,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=3{m}^{5}+4{m}^{4}-1$ is an integer.

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=2{q}^{8}+14{q}^{4}-4,$ where $q\in Z.$ Complete the following argument.

The number $n$ is {{field-1}} since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =2{q}^{8}+14{q}^{4}-4 \\  & =2({{field-2}}-2) \\  & ={{field-3}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=${{field-4}} is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *even* if it can be written as $2a,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Notice that all terms in the expression $2{q}^{8}+14{q}^{4}-4$ have a common factor of $2.$ 

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is $\text{even}$ since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =2{q}^{8}+14{q}^{4}-4 \\  & =2({{{q}^{8}+7{q}^{4}-2}_{⏟}}_{a}) \\  & =2a,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a={q}^{8}+7{q}^{4}-2$ is an integer.

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=-8{p}^{4}+10{p}^{2}+4,$ where $p\in Z.$ Complete the following argument.

The number $n$ is {{field-1}} since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =-8{p}^{4}+10{p}^{2}+4 \\  & =2(-4{p}^{4}+{{field-2}}) \\  & ={{field-3}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=${{field-4}} is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *even* if it can be written as $2a,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Notice that all terms in the expression $-8{p}^{4}+10{p}^{2}+4$ have a common factor of $2.$ 

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is $\text{even}$ since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =-8{p}^{4}+10{p}^{2}+4 \\  & =2({{-4{p}^{4}+5{p}^{2}+2}_{⏟}}_{a}) \\  & =2a,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=-4{p}^{4}+5{p}^{2}+2$ is an integer.

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=8{k}^{6}+8{k}^{3}+16,$ where $k\in Z.$ Complete the following argument.

The number $n$ is {{field-1}} since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =8{k}^{6}+8{k}^{3}+16 \\  & =2({{field-2}}+8) \\  & ={{field-3}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=${{field-4}} is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *even* if it can be written as $2a,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Notice that all terms in the expression $8{k}^{6}+8{k}^{3}+16$ have a common factor of $2.$ 

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is $\text{even}$ since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =8{k}^{6}+8{k}^{3}+16 \\  & =2({{4{k}^{6}+4{k}^{3}+8}_{⏟}}_{a}) \\  & =2a,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=4{k}^{6}+4{k}^{3}+8$ is an integer.

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=8{m}^{3}+12{m}^{2}+10m+2,$ where $m\in Z.$ Complete the following argument.

The number $n$ is {{field-1}} since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =8{m}^{3}+12{m}^{2}+10m+2 \\  & =2(4{m}^{3}+6{m}^{2}+{{field-2}}) \\  & ={{field-3}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=${{field-4}} is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *even* if it can be written as $2a,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Notice that all terms in the expression $8{m}^{3}+12{m}^{2}+10m+2$ have a common factor of $2.$ 

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is $\text{even}$ since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =8{m}^{3}+12{m}^{2}+10m+2 \\  & =2({{4{m}^{3}+6{m}^{2}+5m+1}_{⏟}}_{a}) \\  & =2a,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=4{m}^{3}+6{m}^{2}+5m+1$ is an integer.

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=8pq-4{q}^{8}+4,$ where $p,q\in Z.$ Complete the following argument.

The number $n$ is {{field-1}} since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =8pq-4{q}^{8}+4 \\  & =2({{field-2}}+2) \\  & ={{field-3}},\end{aligned}
$$

where  $a=${{field-4}}.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *even* if it can be written as $2a,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Notice that all terms in the expression $8pq-4{q}^{8}+4$ have a common factor of $2.$ 

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is $\text{even}$ since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =8pq-4{q}^{8}+4 \\  & =2({{4pq-2{q}^{8}+2}_{⏟}}_{a}) \\  & =2a,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=4pq-2{q}^{8}+2\in Z.$

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=-8p+2q+7,$ where $p,q\in Z.$ Complete the following argument.

The number $n$ is {{field-1}} since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =-8p+2q+7 \\  & =2(-4p+{{field-2}})+1 \\  & ={{field-3}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=${{field-4}}.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *odd* if it can be written as $2a+1,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Now, note the following regarding the expression $-8p+2q+7:$

- All terms, apart from the constant term, have a common factor of $2.$

- The constant term can be written as $7=6+1.$

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is $\text{odd}$ since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =-8p+2q+7 \\  & =(-8p+2q+6)+1 \\  & =2({{-4p+q+3}_{⏟}}_{a})+1 \\  & =2a+1,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=-4p+q+3\in Z.$

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=2k+2m-8km-4,$ where $k,m\in Z.$ Complete the following argument.

The number $n$ is {{field-1}} since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =2k+2m-8km-4 \\  & =2({{field-2}}-4km-2) \\  & ={{field-3}},\end{aligned}
$$

where  $a=${{field-4}}.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *even* if it can be written as $2a,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Notice that all terms in the expression $2k+2m-8km-4,$ have a common factor of $2.$ 

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is $\text{even}$ since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =2k+2m-8km-4 \\  & =2({{k+m-4km-2}_{⏟}}_{a}) \\  & =2a,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=k+m-4km-2\in Z.$

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=8k-4m+6,$ where $k,m\in Z.$ Complete the following argument.

The number $n$ is {{field-1}} since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =8k-4m+6 \\  & =2({{field-2}}+3) \\  & ={{field-3}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=${{field-4}}.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *even* if it can be written as $2a,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Notice that all terms in the expression $8k-4m+6$ have a common factor of $2.$ 

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is $\text{even}$ since

$$

questions.problem:
Suppose $n=8-2p-6{q}^{2}-4pq,$ where $p,q\in Z.$ Complete the following argument.

The number $n$ is {{field-1}} since 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =8-2p-6{q}^{2}-4pq \\  & =2(4-{{field-2}}-2pq) \\  & ={{field-3}},\end{aligned}
$$

where  $a=${{field-4}}.
questions.worked_solution:
An integer is *even* if it can be written as $2a,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Notice that all terms in the expression $8-2p-6{q}^{2}-4pq$ have a common factor of $2.$ 

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is $\text{even}$ since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =8-2p-6{q}^{2}-4pq \\  & =2({{4-p-3{q}^{2}-2pq}_{⏟}}_{a}) \\  & =2a,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=4-p-3{q}^{2}-2pq\in Z.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Showing a Linear Expression Is Even
canonical_examples.problem: Suppose $n=10-30p,$ where $p \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Construct an argument that explains why $n$ is even.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An integer is *even* if it can be written as $2a,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is even since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =10-30p \\  & =2({{5-15p}_{⏟}}_{a}) \\  & =2a,\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}5-15p},$ which is an integer.

Example: 
                    Showing a Linear Expression Is Odd
canonical_examples.problem: Suppose $n=3-4m,$ where $m \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Construct an argument that explains why $n$ is odd.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An integer is *odd* if it can be written as $2a + 1,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is *odd* since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =3-4m \\  & =(-4m+2)+1 \\  & =2({{-2m+1}_{⏟}}_{a})+1 \\  & =2a+1,\end{aligned}
$$

where we have defined $a=\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-2m+1},$ which is an integer.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Proving Parity of Non-Linear Expressions
canonical_examples.problem: Suppose $n=4m^2+2m-1,$ where $m \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Construct an argument that explains why $n$ is odd.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An integer is *odd* if it can be written as $2a + 1,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Now, note the following regarding the expression $4m^2+2m-1{:}$

- All terms, apart from the constant term, have a common factor of $2.$

- The constant term can be written as $-1 = -2+1.$

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{odd}}$ since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =4{m}^{2}+2m-1 \\  & =(4{m}^{2}+2m-2)+1 \\  & =2({{2{m}^{2}+m-1}_{⏟}}_{a})+1 \\  & =2a+1,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a=\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2m^2+m-1}$ is an integer.

Example: 
                    Proving Parity of Non-Linear Expressions With Multiple Variables
canonical_examples.problem: Suppose $n=2pq - 4q + 5,$ where $p,q \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Construct an argument that explains why $n$ is odd.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An integer is *odd* if it can be written as $2a + 1,$ where $a$ is an integer.

Now, note the following regarding the expression $2pq - 4q + 5 {:}$

- All terms, apart from the constant term, have a common factor of $2.$

- The constant term can be written as $5 = 4+1.$

Therefore, we complete our argument as follows:

The number $n$ is $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{odd}}$ since

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =2pq-4q+5 \\  & =(2pq-4q+4)+1 \\  & =2({{pq-2q+2}_{⏟}}_{a})+1 \\  & =2a+1,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a= \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue} pq - 2q + 2\in \mathbb Z }.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to prove universal statements that involve the evenness and oddness of simple expressions. 

First, we have the following definitions:

- Two integers have the **same parity** if they're *both* even or *both* odd.

- Two integers have **opposite parity** if *one* of them is even and the *other* is odd.

For example:

- The integers $2$ and $4$ have the *same* parity because they're both even.

- The integers $1$ and $7$ have the *same* parity because they're both odd.

- On the other hand, the integers $1$ and $6$ have *opposite* parity because $1$ is odd and $6$ is even.

tutorials.name: Representing Even Integers
tutorials.problem:
The list below gives the first few even integers:

$$
0, \quad \pm 2, \quad \pm 4, \quad \pm 6, \quad \pm 8, \quad \ldots
$$

An integer is even if it is a multiple of $2.$ And, since every integer is a multiple of its factors, every even integer can be written as 

$$
{\color{red}{2}}\times {\color{blue}{\textrm{some other integer}}}.
$$

For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =2\times 0 \\ 2 & =2\times 1 \\ 4 & =2\times 2 \\ 12 & =2\times 6 \\ -24 & =2\times (-12)\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose we know that an integer $n$ is even. Then, we can rewrite $n$ as follows:

$$
n={\color{red}{2}}{\color{blue}{a}}
$$

where ${\color{blue}{a}}$ is an integer. 

This choice of letter for the second factor is arbitrary: we chose ${\color{blue}{a}}$ here, but we can use any letter we like! However, the following variables are commonly used to denote integers:

$$
a, \quad b, \quad c, \quad k, \quad l, \quad m, \quad n, \quad p, \quad q, \quad r, \quad x, \quad y, \quad z
$$

tutorials.name: Showing an Expression Is Even
tutorials.problem:
Consider the following statement:

$\qquad$ $P:\: \forall n\in\mathbb Z,\, 8n-4$ *is even.*

To prove this statement, we need to show that $8n-4$ can be written as $2{\color{blue}{a}},$ where ${\color{blue}{a}}$ is an integer. 

The first step is to factor out $2$ from the expression.

$$
8n-4 = 2(4n-2)
$$

Next, we introduce a new variable ${\color{blue}{a}},$ where

$$
{\color{blue}{a}} = 4n-2.
$$

Notice that since $n\in\mathbb Z,$ we have that $4n-2\in\mathbb Z.$ In other words, ${\color{blue}{a}}\in\mathbb Z.$ It's essential to state this since the whole argument breaks down if the second factor is sometimes not an integer. 

Now, our expression can be written as

$$
2(4n-2) = 2{\color{blue}{a}}.
$$

So, since $8n-4$ can be written in the form $2{\color{blue}{a}}$ where ${\color{blue}{a}}$ is an integer, we conclude that $8n-4$ is even *for all* $n\in\mathbb Z.$

Let's take a look at another example. Before we do, note that statements about parity are often written informally, and so the universal quantifier $\forall$ is usually hidden.

tutorials.name: Representing Odd Integers
tutorials.problem:
Recall that an integer is *odd* if it is not even. The list below gives the first few odd integers:

$$
\pm 1, \quad \pm 3, \quad \pm 5, \quad \pm 7, \quad \ldots
$$

Notice that every odd integer can be expressed as 

$$
{\color{red}{2}}\times {\color{blue}{\textrm{some other integer}}} + 1.
$$

For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =2\times 0+1 \\ 3 & =2\times 1+1 \\ 5 & =2\times 2+1 \\ 19 & =2\times 9+1 \\ -17 & =2\times (-9)+1\end{aligned}
$$

In general, an integer $n$ is odd if it can be written as 

$$
n={\color{red}{2}}{\color{blue}{a}}+1
$$

where $\color{blue}a$ is an integer.
